html:
A film that goes straight to the heart. To me, a successful film doesn’t teach you how to live, still less chase a happy ending. It lets you see clearly the helplessness of life and of human nature, strikes a chord, projects itself naturally onto your own life and gets you thinking.

Kudos to Hailu Qin. I knew very little about her before, but a while ago I watched The Piano in a Factory (yes, I’m that late to the party…). Her performance was stunning, and her Best Actress award was thoroughly deserved.

I meant to write just a couple of lines, but this film is such a rare gem among Chinese films that I want to say more.

What struck me most were the helplessness of human nature and of life, and how completely the film puts you in its characters’ shoes.

Films rarely move me like this. On the one hand, there aren’t many great Chinese films (or maybe I’ve seen too few). In an age when traffic is king, even trashing a bad show can bring in plenty of traffic; it really is a strange world. On the other hand, there are lots of good foreign films, from Japan, Korea, the US and Europe, but cultural differences make it hard to feel a strong connection.

This film resonated with me intensely.

The oppressive mood is set from the very start: the restless handheld camera, the lonely life of an empty-nester, the modest home, the old woman’s suspicious expressions and her late husband, who keeps appearing. It’s oppressive, with a hint of horror. In the first act, when the old woman keeps getting anonymous phone calls, I guessed the story was set in the late 1980s or early 1990s. The walls painted half green and half white, the old landline phone, the furnishings: it all looked just like many of the homes I remember from primary school.

But as the story went on, I noticed that the car Hailu Qin drives definitely isn’t from that era, and I began to wonder. Then I saw the younger son’s Apple computer and knew for sure that it was set in the present. That’s the beauty of not reading spoilers: I was completely drawn into the story.

The scene of the old woman soaking her feet in a foot basin touched me deeply. Maybe it’s because my parents also soak their feet in a basin, or because I once bought a foot basin for my wife’s grandmother. Either way, it’s full of everyday life; as people say these days, it’s really down-to-earth. Then the old woman alone in the dimly lit room, the flickering light of the TV playing across her face, the cheerful noise coming from it: loneliness could hardly be brought out more starkly. Her behavior, her clothes, the way she talks, every gesture captures the image of countless Chinese men and women in their seventies and eighties. The permed, graying curls, the floral-print clothes, the towel blanket, the palm-leaf fan on the coffee table, the fly swatter hanging by the door, the way she always leans forward and presses the remote with both hands: anyone who grew up with their grandparents will find it all deeply familiar.

The sets are spot on and the acting is masterly. Watching these scenes, I couldn’t help thinking of my own grandmother, my mother’s mother. She is nearly 90 and has mild to moderate dementia. She used to dote on us grandchildren more than anyone; a few years ago she started mixing up our names, and now she hardly remembers them at all. I grew up with her, and when the symptoms first appeared I was heartbroken. A few years on, I’ve gradually got used to it. I don’t ask after her as often as I used to, maybe because, deep down, I know she’s no longer the grandmother she was and I’ll never get any response from her again. That helplessness is the same as that of the elder son’s family and the younger son in the film. We grow up, leave home and live far from our families. As teenagers we can’t bear to leave home; a decade or more later we’ve drifted apart and become strangers. I still remember the end of my first National Day holiday at college. My grandmother saw me off before I got on the bus, and as she walked away she kept turning back to look at me, until she couldn’t hold back her tears, turned her face away to wipe them, and never looked back again… In the blink of an eye, more than ten years have gone by.

That is the helplessness of living, or of life itself. There is also the helplessness of the elder son’s family, torn between filial duty and the realities of their own lives; of the younger son, whose personality clashes with conventional values; and of the old woman, sent down to the countryside for decades and left with nothing to show for a lifetime.

Another kind of helplessness is that of human nature.

The helplessness of the old woman, who would wreck another family’s happiness for the sake of her own, and who breaks the law to make amends for a wrong that has haunted her all her life; and the helplessness of the little boy, wavering between hatred and the goodness in human nature. Even as we sigh over them, we can’t hate the old woman or the boy, because everyone is selfish. That kind of resonance makes you think hard.

If the film has a lesson, I think it’s this: when you face a choice in life, think it over carefully and try to make a decision you won’t regret. Even if things don’t turn out as you expected, you’ll be able to accept it and bear it. And meet life with love; live it earnestly and work hard at it.
